title: How to Run a Print Quality Audit Before Scaling a Subliminator Design
excerpt: A repeatable quality check for all-over print sellers: sample the right units, score them against a fixed rubric, and decide whether a design is genuinely ready for paid traffic.
body: The most expensive mistake in print on demand is not a bad design. It is putting ad spend behind a design that prints inconsistently, so every new order generates another support ticket and another refund. A one hour audit before you scale is cheaper than a week of damage control. The point is not to inspect every unit forever, but to prove that a specific design on a specific blank produces a predictable result before you let paid traffic loose on it.

Start by buying your own product. Supplier mockups and the sample you saw at launch are not evidence of current production. Order three units of the exact variant you plan to advertise, spaced a few days apart so you are not looking at one production batch alone, and have them shipped to yourself rather than to a friend. Subliminator handles cutting, sewing and printing in one flow, which means you are auditing the whole chain at once rather than a single decorative step.

Score what arrives against a fixed rubric instead of a general impression. Check colour accuracy against the file you uploaded, especially in the darkest and lightest areas where all over print tends to shift. Check placement at the seams, since panels that meet slightly off register are visible on the finished garment in a way that never shows in a flat mockup. Check fabric hand feel and stretch recovery, then wash one unit twice and re-score it. Write a single number from one to five for each line so you can compare across designs and across months.

Decide what a failing score means before you see the results. A rubric without a decision rule is just an opinion. Set the thresholds in advance: anything under four on colour or placement goes back to the file for correction, anything under three on wash durability gets pulled from the catalog entirely, and anything that fails twice on the same line gets dropped as a supplier fit problem rather than a design problem. Pre-committing keeps you from rationalising a three because the design is already live.

Connect the audit to the numbers you already watch. Tag orders for each audited design and compare refund rate, size exchange rate and repeat purchase rate against the score you recorded. Within a quarter you will know whether a score of four actually predicts a clean order, and you can tighten the rubric accordingly. This is also the fastest way to find the designs that sell well but generate disproportionate support load, which are usually the ones where the mockup over-promises.

Make it a gate, not a one-off project. Any design about to receive its first real budget passes the audit first, and any design that changes blanks or print method passes again. Keep the scores in a simple sheet, because drift over time is the real signal: a design that scored five in spring and four in autumn is telling you something changed upstream.
